Reposting message from <@U02LAK62DEV> in this channel:

Hooray! our Civic Ep and print, *Tenants Organize to Keep Building Affordable Through Nonprofit Purchase* from *Dec 2019* is featured in today's Solutions Journalism newsletter  whichj i recommend subscribing to for SoJo approach to everything...

*Tenant organizing to maintain affordability*
Growing up, my visits to New York City (from California) consisted of sleeping on my great aunt’s floor in her Upper West Side apartment that she’s lived in since 1964. With orange shag carpet and brick walls, the one bedroom is rent controlled, allowing her to stay in the same place for almost 60 years for under $900 a month, even as the prices of the neighborhood skyrocketed around her. Now in her 80s, she’ll be able to stay in her home as long as she physically can, while rents in Manhattan have recently topped $5,000, the highest ever.
Now I live in Colorado, where rent control is prohibited by state law and taken off the table in any discussion around housing affordability. So it’s got me thinking, are there other solutions to keeping rent affordable that may be more palatable to jurisdictions across the country?
To start, resources about landlords can give tenants pertinent information before they ever sign a lease, and help weed out highly priced units. A ProPublica environmental reporter recently wrote a how-to guide about <https://solutionsjournalism.us1.list-manage.com/track/click?u=08368885cad8bf75d17e3863a&id=1bdce97b47&e=65130b2038|researching landlords> in New York City. Journalists at Outlier Media took the idea and created a similar guide for Detroiters:<https://solutionsjournalism.us1.list-manage.com/track/click?u=08368885cad8bf75d17e3863a&id=2c227077cc&e=65130b2038| How to research a Detroit landlord — and spot red flags before you sign a lease>. Although both of these are city-specific, they have plenty of pointers about finding — or advocating for — similar information in your own town.
When it comes to rising prices of current units, tenant organizing has been used to secure affordability in some of the most expensive cities in the country. Earlier this year, The New York Times broke down how <https://solutionsjournalism.us1.list-manage.com/track/click?u=08368885cad8bf75d17e3863a&id=e46b1e8583&e=65130b2038|a group of tenants> came together to buy their building in the Bronx. After threats of high rent increases, the residents pursued the purchase through a limited equity co-op model, securing their units for a purchase price of $2,500 each. <https://solutionsjournalism.us1.list-manage.com/track/click?u=08368885cad8bf75d17e3863a&id=2181ea1403&e=65130b2038|Tenants in a San Francisco> building organized and partnered with a nonprofit to buy their property from the landlord so that they could maintain their rent in a very expensive city.

Are renters in your region organizing to protect themselves from rising costs? Are your towns and cities implementing policies to keep rent affordable for the working class? Innovative solutions are being tried and tested all around us — and could inform your audience and community.
_Angela K. Evans, Labor Cohort Manager_

attachments.fallback: A Landlord ‘Underestimated’ His Tenants. Now They Could Own the Building.
attachments.text: When a new landlord bought their building in the Bronx and threatened to raise rents and kick them out, tenants banded together. They never expected how far they might get: the chance to buy their apartments for $2,500 each.
attachments.title: A Landlord ‘Underestimated’ His Tenants. Now They Could Own the Building.
